data.sourcePassage:
Victorian Britain was the Britain of Queen Victoria's reign, from 1837 to 1901. It was a period of huge change. Britain became more urban, more industrial and more powerful in the wider world. Railways, factories, docks, mines and expanding towns changed how millions of people lived and worked.

Victorian society was unequal. The upper classes owned land and inherited wealth. The middle classes included factory owners, merchants, professionals and shopkeepers. The working classes included factory workers, miners, dock workers, servants and labourers. Class affected where people lived, what work they did, what education they received and their access to medical care.

Victorian respectability was important, especially for the middle classes. Respectable people were expected to be hard-working, sober, religious and orderly. However, respectability could lead some Victorians to blame poor people for their own poverty, even when low wages, unemployment and illness were the real causes. Women were also unequal: middle-class women were expected to focus on the home, while working-class women had to earn money as well as care for children. Women had fewer legal and political rights than men for most of this period.

Industrial towns grew quickly, but housing often did not keep pace with population growth. Common problems in working-class areas included overcrowded houses, shared privies, open drains, polluted water pumps and factory smoke. These conditions helped diseases spread. Cholera, typhus, typhoid, tuberculosis and smallpox were major dangers. At first, many people saw public health as a private matter, but it gradually became clear that disease did not respect class boundaries.

questions.question: What did Victorian 'respectability' sometimes lead people to do?
options: Campaign for voting rights for working-class men
Blame poor people for their own poverty, even when low wages and illness were the real causes
Donate all their wealth to the poor
Support the building of large workhouses in every town
questions.modelAnswer: Respectability could lead some Victorians to blame poor people for poverty, even when the real causes were low wages, unemployment and illness.

questions.question: Why did industrial towns have serious public health problems?
options: Governments banned the building of sewers in industrial areas
Working-class people chose to live in unhealthy conditions
Housing could not keep pace with rapid population growth, leading to overcrowding, polluted water and poor drainage
Disease was always worse in rural areas than in towns
questions.modelAnswer: Housing did not keep pace with rapid population growth. This led to overcrowding, shared privies, open drains and polluted water pumps that helped diseases spread.

questions.question: The passage says disease 'did not respect class boundaries'. Why was this important for public health reform?
options: It showed that the middle classes should move to the countryside
It helped persuade middle-class and upper-class people that disease in poor areas was also a danger to them
It proved that working-class people were more vulnerable to all diseases
It showed that public health was a private matter best left to charities
questions.modelAnswer: If disease could spread from poor districts to wealthier areas, middle-class and upper-class people had a direct interest in supporting public health reform. This helped build wider political support for improvements.

data.section: Cholera, Chadwick and Public Health Reform
data.sourceTitle: Reformers, Evidence and the Fight Against Cholera
data.targetTitle: Reformers, Evidence and the Fight Against Cholera
data.sourcePassage:
Cholera terrified Victorians because it could kill quickly. Britain had major cholera outbreaks in 1832, 1848-49 and 1853-54. Miasma theory was popular because cholera often appeared in dirty, smelly districts. Bad smells seemed like visible evidence of unhealthy conditions, even if smell itself was not the cause of cholera.

Edwin Chadwick published an important report in 1842 on sanitary conditions in Britain. It used evidence from doctors, local officials and statistics to show that people in unhealthy towns often died younger than those in cleaner areas. Chadwick argued that dirty conditions caused disease, that clean water and proper drainage would reduce illness, and that public health reform would save money in the long run. His work helped lead to the 1848 Public Health Act, which allowed local boards of health to be created. However, the Act was not strong enough, and many towns did not act because the law was mostly voluntary.

John Snow was a doctor who investigated the 1854 cholera outbreak in Soho, London. He mapped deaths and noticed many victims had used water from the Broad Street pump. Snow argued cholera was spread through contaminated water, not bad air. When the pump handle was removed, the outbreak declined. Snow's investigation mattered because it used careful evidence and mapping to challenge miasma theory and link disease to a specific source.

The Great Stink of 1858 — when the polluted River Thames smelled terrible near Parliament in hot weather — pushed politicians to support Joseph Bazalgette's major sewer system for London. The much stronger 1875 Public Health Act made local authorities responsible for clean water, sewers, rubbish collection and disease prevention. It made public health a normal responsibility of local government.

questions.question: What did Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report argue?
options: That cholera was spread by miasma from the River Thames
That dirty conditions caused disease and that clean water and drainage would reduce illness
That the Poor Law should be abolished immediately
That vaccination should be made compulsory for all children
questions.modelAnswer: Chadwick argued that dirty conditions caused disease and that clean water, proper drainage and public health reform would reduce illness and save money.

questions.question: How did John Snow investigate the 1854 cholera outbreak?
options: He studied bacteria under a microscope to identify the cause
He mapped cholera deaths and identified the Broad Street water pump as the source
He examined patients in hospital to find a common symptom
He interviewed cholera survivors about their diet and lifestyle
questions.modelAnswer: Snow mapped the deaths from cholera in Soho and noticed that many victims had used water from the Broad Street pump, leading him to link the disease to contaminated water.

questions.question: Why was the 1848 Public Health Act limited in its impact?
options: Parliament voted to repeal it in 1849
It only applied to London and not to the rest of Britain
Much of the action it allowed was voluntary, so many towns did not act
It was declared unconstitutional by the courts
questions.modelAnswer: The 1848 Act allowed but did not require local boards to act. Because much action was voluntary, many towns chose not to improve sanitation.

questions.question: The passage shows both the 1848 and 1875 Public Health Acts. What does comparing them suggest about how public health reform developed?
options: Reform was instant and complete after the 1848 Act
Reform was gradual and required stronger laws as earlier voluntary measures proved insufficient
The 1848 Act was stronger and more effective than the 1875 Act
Both Acts had identical powers and achieved the same results
questions.modelAnswer: The 1848 Act was limited and mostly voluntary, so many towns did not improve. The 1875 Act was much stronger and made public health a legal responsibility of local government. This shows reform was gradual, moving from weak voluntary measures to stronger legal requirements.

data.section: Poverty, Workhouses and the Limits of Reform
data.sourceTitle: Poverty, Workhouses and the Limits of Victorian Reform
data.targetTitle: Poverty, Workhouses and the Limits of Victorian Reform
data.sourcePassage:
The 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act changed poor relief in England and Wales. It aimed to reduce the cost of helping the poor by making the workhouse central to the system. People who entered workhouses received food and shelter, but conditions were deliberately harsh. Families were separated, routines were strict and the work was often unpleasant. Supporters argued that workhouses stopped idleness and kept costs down. Critics argued that they punished poverty rather than dealing with its causes.

Victorian debates about poverty divided between individual and structural explanations. Individual explanations claimed poverty was caused by laziness, drinking or poor choices. Structural explanations pointed to low wages, unsafe work, illness, disability and lack of education as the real causes. Many Victorians believed in self-help — the idea that individuals should improve their lives through hard work and discipline. Philanthropy, or charitable giving, tried to help through model housing, schools, hospitals and soup kitchens. Charity could reduce suffering, but it could not replace nationwide reform.

Victorian reform improved many lives. Some towns built better sewers and cleaner water supplies. New laws limited child labour and expanded schooling. Death rates from some diseases eventually fell. Public parks, baths and libraries appeared in some areas.

However, problems continued. Overcrowding remained serious, slum housing survived into the twentieth century, poverty continued despite charity, and women and poorer people had limited political power throughout the period. The best judgement about Victorian reform is balanced: there were important improvements in sanitation, law and local government, but the improvements were not immediate, equal or complete.

questions.question: What were workhouses in Victorian Britain?
options: Factories where workers were paid high wages for skilled labour
Institutions where poor people could receive basic food and shelter in return for work in deliberately harsh conditions
Schools where working-class children received free education
Hospitals providing free medical care to the poor
questions.modelAnswer: Workhouses were institutions where poor people could receive basic food and shelter in return for work. Conditions were deliberately harsh to discourage people from claiming poor relief.

questions.question: What is the difference between individual and structural explanations for poverty?
options: Individual explanations blame society; structural explanations blame the poor person
Individual explanations blame the poor person's choices; structural explanations point to low wages, illness and unfair conditions
Both explanations are identical and came to the same conclusions
Individual explanations support workhouses; structural explanations support charity
questions.modelAnswer: Individual explanations claimed poverty was caused by laziness or poor choices. Structural explanations pointed to low wages, unsafe work, illness and lack of education as the real causes.

questions.question: Why could philanthropy not solve poverty on its own?
options: Victorian charities had too much money and created dependency
Philanthropy was illegal under the 1834 Poor Law
Charity could reduce suffering for some, but it could not replace nationwide reform of wages, housing and working conditions
Victorian people refused to donate to charities
questions.modelAnswer: Charity could reduce suffering for some people, but it could not change the structural causes of poverty such as low wages, unsafe housing and lack of education. Nationwide reform was needed for lasting change.

questions.question: The passage concludes that a 'balanced' judgement is needed on Victorian reform. What does this mean?
options: Victorian reform either completely succeeded or completely failed
Victorian reform made important improvements but was not immediate, equal or complete for everyone
Victorian reform had no effect at all on working-class lives
Victorian reform succeeded perfectly by 1901
questions.modelAnswer: A balanced judgement acknowledges both sides: there were important improvements in sanitation, law and local government, but overcrowding, slum housing and poverty continued, and benefits were not shared equally across society.
